Outcome: Depression cases (lower is better)

## Study A
Found: benefit
Claim: Women with vitamin D below 20 ng/ml were 3.3 times more likely to have postpartum depression than women with vitamin D above 20 ng/ml.
Sentence: "Women with vitamin D less than 20ng/ml compared to vitamin D > 20ng/ml were 3.30 times more likely to have postpartum depression (OR: 3.3, CI: 1.32-8.24, p= 0.01)."
Measured as: postpartum depression
Population: 120 reproductive-aged Iranian women in Izeh, Iran, 60 with postpartum depression and 60 without
Intervention: Serum 25-OH vitamin D level measured by ELISA (observational, no intervention)
Comparator: Vitamin D above 20 ng/ml
Design: case-control study
Sample size: 120
baseline_vitamin_d_status: mixed

## Study B
Found: no effect
Claim: Lifetime diagnosis of major depressive disorder was not significantly associated with vitamin D concentrations.
Sentence: "Symptoms of depression and the lifetime diagnosis of MDD were not significantly associated with vitamin D concentrations."
Measured as: lifetime diagnosis of MDD (CID-S)
Population: General population sample from the Study of Health in Pomerania (SHIP-1)
Intervention: Serum 25(OH)D level (measured, not given)
Comparator: Lower versus higher vitamin D levels
Design: cross-sectional study
Sample size: 1,908
baseline_vitamin_d_status: not_reported

content.text: {"rationale":"Both findings concern vitamin D exposure and depression, but Study A is a postpartum case-control in women with a 3.3-fold odds, while Study B is a cross-sectional general-population lifetime MDD diagnosis; the disagreement stems from population and design.","verdict":"genuine","reason":"population","also_differs":["design_or_bias"],"detail":"population: 120 postpartum Iranian women (60 cases) vs 1,908 general German adults; design: case-control vs cross-sectional"}
